utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd like to ask Madam Usher to escort into the courtroom first counsel, then the witness, Mr. Mandic, unless there's any procedural issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There is one procedural matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's one thing I thought I could deal with, taking into account how much time it usually takes to get the witness into the courtroom, and that is, I would like to ask Mr. Stewart how much time he would need for any observations or submissions in relation to material that arrived on the desk of the secretaries of the Judges and has not reached the desks of the Judges themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I feel fairly confident I can make my points in less than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then deal do that at the end of this first session, just before the break. Then we'll stop five minutes earlier. Mr. Tieger, is there anything you'd like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This relates to the matter raised yesterday in connection with the disclosure of documents. Let me begin by noting that I have absolutely no intention of reopening or re-arguing that motion, but last night we went through a recalculation of the documents disclosed. I notified Mr. Stewart about that recalculation, and he graciously suggested or agreed that we should at least bring that clarification to the Court. In sum, it appears that the calculation of the number of documents disclosed, based on gigabytes, yields an inaccurate number, for a variety of reasons, including the fact that it contains TIF files versus Word documents, which have considerably more gigabytes and the fact that they were video and audio files contained in there as well. Our support staff instituted a recalculation based on ERN ranges, and of the number of documents, of those documents which are in excess of ten pages, and those calculations produced a number of disclosed pages of approximately 1.600, somewhere under 2.000, rather than the 25.000 that were indicated yesterday. And so in keeping with my discussions with Mr. Stewart, we agreed that we'd bring those enhanced, refined figures to the attention of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand that the parties discussed that the number was lower, but still a considerable number of pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In fact, the discussion took place -- I mean, we understand that Mr. Curiam spent some considerable time, we understand, yesterday doing this exercise. I received an e-mail from Mr. Tieger yesterday evening, and I responded to it in the terms which he's just summarised last night. There were one or two exclusions or exceptions to that figure that Mr. Tieger has given, but we suggest that we don't spend any more time on this this morning, Your Honour. We can spend a bit of time checking some of them. When I say checking, we're not doubting Mr. Acrilan's work, but is just seeing how it fits into the picture. So that's where we are at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is grateful that the parties expect the Judges to understand the difference between a Word file and a TIF file. Then, Madam Usher, could I ask you to escort first counsel and then the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: One more thing, it won't take a second. I don't have a problem with the witness being in court. It was just that Ms. Cmeric overnight, she was troubled yesterday, as she is sometimes by discrepancies in translation, looking at the English statements of the interviews of this witness and the B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Her troubled nature hasn't calmed down overnight because as she is looked at it, she has found significant discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ask Mr. Mandic to be seated. He was still standing. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, for not raising this a moment ago. It's just that, Your Honour; and our concern is we have found what Ms. Cmeric regards as significant discrepancies. It's that when passages in the statement or critical passages are put to the witness, we suggest that perhaps a witness should be provided with the B/C/S version of the statement. Alternatively -- well, I'm trying to think what an alternative is. But, well, yes, Your Honour. Excuse me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take the opportunity, Mr. Mandic, to say good morning to you. We'll finish this procedural issue in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Excuse me. I was just confirming what the system was here. Yes. We suggest that the witness is provided with the B/C/S statement, because we understand that the B/C/S version of these interviews is a transcription of the tape-recording of what the witness said in B/C/S in the original interview. And of course, it was interpreted. And that the English version of the -- the English version of the interviews is a transcription of what was said by the interpreter. Mr. Margetts was actually there, but that's what we understand as being the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that the questions, the English is the original, and answers, the B/C/S version might be the original, the most directly linked to what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. That must be right, Your Honour. But Mr. Margetts was actually present at these, and so was Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That part is certainly correct. It wouldn't answer the question of how the transcription took place. The transcription can be either --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We can discuss a lot, but the matter is whether there's any important difference in language in one language or the other. Would you mind to -- that the witness has the B/C/S version of the transcript, if that's available, in front of him when his attention is drawn to certain parts of his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, of course I wouldn't mind, Your Honour. However, that is assuming that Mr. Stewart's understanding of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- what is represents is correct. Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever happens, it's always important to find out that there is inconsistency in language in one version or another, and we'll then, if we are confronted with that, of course we'll have to find out what's the most reliable version and what's the real version. And we'll solve that then. But let's start with --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm also trying to determine whether we have the transcription in B/C/S for the second interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was one of my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Cmeric has got what we understood to be that, Your Honour. Just to clarify - I hope perhaps in my own mind as well - what's happening otherwise is that something which was originally said by Mr. Mandic at the interview in B/C/S was interpreted, it was translated into English then and is now being translated back again by the interpreters in this court. So it's introducing two steps. And the result is considerable discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if your assumption is right, then of course the inferences you've drawn are right as well. Whether they're right or not, we'll find out, because there will be an audiotape anyhow. So that if there's any problem about what the witness really said when he gave his statement, we'll always have an opportunity to check that. Let's get started and let's see how it goes. Do we have B/C/S versions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At least one copy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I understand the Defence has the are other one and is willing to make that available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. Can I just mentioned in 15 seconds. We also are troubled by a number of points in the statement where we come across unintelligible. We'll look into that further to see the scale of that difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed yesterday when we listened to a telephone intercept that something that was -- that could not be heard in the transcript, that our interpreters were able to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. We'll investigate that a bit further, Your Honour, because we're a bit concerned about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honour, although it will become apparent at least during the course of this morning's session if we attempt to use the transcript, there are no line-reference numbers on these transcripts, as I think Mr. Stewart is aware. And the page numbers will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We'll have to solve that problem. Mr. Tieger -- first of all, Mr. Mandic, Mr. Tieger will now resume his examination-in-chief. I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, just before we recessed yesterday, I had asked you about the development of any rivalry between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, and you had responded that after a few years of the war, there was a kind of rivalry that sprang up and a stratification among people as to who was closer to one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I had been about to present you with a document, and I'll do that now. That's B008-4249, Prosecution's next in order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P414.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'll give you a moment to review that document, which is a draft official note from the security services centre at Banja Luka, prepared in June of 1993, referring in particular to contacts with individuals from the National Security Service and military security. And I want to direct your attention in particular to a portion that appears on page 3 of the English, which is the portion of the third full paragraph of the document. That's the paragraph that begins: "Through the contacts with Markovic ..." And it refers to some of the comments of Markovic, including: "When speaking of the leaders of the Republika Srpska including Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, Markovic and his proteges used extremely abusive terms that degraded and belittled these two leaders of the Serbian people. It is interesting that their comments indicated that there was a subdued struggle for domination between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik." And then the document does go on to include other comments by Markovic and other rumours regarding Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik. I wanted to ask you, however, whether that document reflects, and the comments that I just referred to, reflect the rivalry that you referred to in your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this document. I don't know who this Mr. Markovic is at all. I don't think that Karadzic or Krajisnik liked some parts of Republika Srpska more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that comment you just made, I presume, refers to a comment in the document by Markovic about Mr. Krajisnik's negative attitude toward Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Apart from that, Mr. Mandic, does the comment about the struggle for domination, a subdued struggle for domination, the document reads, between Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic, reflect the view that a rivalry had developed between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that, thanks to some people who were in the immediate vicinity of one or the other, there were latent misunderstandings, or rather, subdued rivalry between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you've indicated, and we've just touched on the existence of people who were identified with or close to one or the other of these two leaders. Were you friends with or closely identified with one or the other?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was close to Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, yesterday we looked at the minutes of a meeting of the Council of Ministers, which included an agenda item referring to the priorities springing from the promulgation -- the declaration of the promulgation of the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that included the defining of ethnic territory and the establishment of government organs.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Bosnian Serb authorities begin to move forward, at least in part, to ensure that Serbian power was felt in the territories claimed by the Bosnian Serb authorities by organising a Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me show you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Someone is typing near a microphone which gives us the constant sound of typing. If there would be another technical solution for that, it would be fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, may I ask you to look at the Prosecution's next exhibit in order. That's SA00-6590.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may make a suggestion. Sometimes two mouse-pads under the keyboard helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the exhibit now in front of you, P415, reflects the minutes of a meeting held in Banja Luka on 11 February 1992. And the first paragraph indicates the attendees at that meeting, including yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those persons were the leading Bosnian Serb officials in the -- in what was at that time the unified MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if I could direct your attention to the second speaker, Mr. Stanisic, whose comments appear in the second paragraph. Mr. Stanisic referred, did he not, to the position of the Ministerial Council, the position of the Council of Ministers?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that position was that in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina which is under Serbian power, this power has to be felt; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Stanisic then went on to state that work should be done on the organisation of a Serbian MUP, starting with municipal and regional branches, to the Serbian ministry itself.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, the leaders of the Serb people in the joint MUP, Mr. Stanisic, he informed us about the decisions of the Assembly and the Ministerial Council, and Mico Stanisic was a member of that council, as the future minister, and he told us what the decisions of the ministerial council were, the ones that were held -- from the meeting held before this meeting. He told us about the establishment of the Serb MUPs in municipalities where there was a majority Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Radovic, speaking after Mr. Stanisic, discussed the decision of the Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to the establishment of a Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Before this meeting, the Assembly of the Serb People in the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina reached a decision on the establishment of a Serb MUP, and I think that on that occasion a law was passed, a law on the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, later on during the course of this meeting, and I would direct your attention to the comments of Mr. Tutus, there was an expression of the loss of confidence in the Serbian leadership of the MUP and the expression of trust in you, as the MUP representative.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Tutus probably meant coordination and cooperation with the headquarters of the joint MUP in Sarajevo. Actually, before the war, Krajina was territorial, or rather, organisationally separated from Sarajevo. They had their headquarters in Banja Luka. There was already the reflex of the war from Croatia that was spilling over into Krajina, which bordered on the then Serb Republic of Krajina, which was in Croatia. And then there was poor cooperation between Banja Luka and Sarajevo, and there were already disagreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Tutus was reflecting those disagreements in his comments, but indicating that he and others from Bosnian Krajina had trust in you, as an individual?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's exactly the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the meeting reached certain conclusions, which appear to be contained on page 4 of the English translation and are headed "Conclusions," including the following: That a Serbian advisory board would be established at the joint MUP, consisting of the Serbian staff in leading positions; that that advisory board would be headed by you, who would ensure that conclusions were acted upon and carried out; that the Serbian advisory board was ordered to carry out all the necessary preparations for the functioning of the Serbian MUP, following the adoption of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that not a single decision on the personnel policy in the joint MUP would be carried out without the prior consent of yourself.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course there are other conclusions, as we can see from the page, but those are the ones I wanted to bring your attention to. Now, following this meeting, Mr. Mandic, you followed up by taking steps to discharge the responsibilities which you had received at the meeting by instructing leading Bosnian Serb officials to move forward in that process; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me present you with Prosecution's next exhibit in order. That's 0063-7176.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, it's a very short document, dated February 13th, 1992, two days after the man Banja Luka meeting, that refers to the conclusions reached at that meeting, and it is signed by you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it was you were instructing those to whom the document was directed to do?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to act in accordance with the conclusions from the previous document, the one that we read a few moments ago. That means that according to the decision of the Ministerial Council and the Assembly of the Serb People, a decision was reached to organise a Serbian MUP, and Goran Radovic and Mico Stanisic informed us about these decisions. He was a member of the Ministerial Council. So we passed a decision in that respect and we acted upon it. This is an obligation that we had because, as assistant minister, I'm the only one who had a 02 line then, and I could send telegrams throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the highest-ranking Serb person in the joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And to whom was this document directed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was directed to the heads of the centres. The security centres of Banja Luka, Nevesinje, Sokolac, Doboj, Gorazde, Nevesinje, Sokolac, and Sarajevo. These are the major security centres in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, did some of the steps toward the preparation for separation of the joint MUP, or unified MUP, include arming of Serbian police stations or police officials and at least the beginnings of terminations of non-Serbs from police forces?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was the other way around then. Up until the beginning of the war, in the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were about 11.000 members of the MUP. From among them -- among them, there were 75 per cent Serbs. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was mainly Serbs who were in the army and police, which did not correspond to the ethnic pattern of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So conclusions were reached by the senior staff of the MUP to dismiss Serb personnel who were trained and educated to work on this kind of job, and that Bosniaks and Croats should be recruited from elsewhere, including the reserve force and the Territorial Defence, so that this pattern would correspond with the ethnic pattern in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That means that at that time, there were more Serbs on the force than there were in Bosnia-Herzegovina itself, and that is one of the problems that was faced by the joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we'll touch upon that issue perhaps a bit later. Let me return to the question I asked before, and that is whether or not there was -- there were efforts by Bosnian Serb officials to arm Serbian police, provide arms to Serbian police, and whether or not the beginning of terminations of non-Serbs from police forces began prior to the onset of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, those would really be better, we suggest, as two separate questions. They're quite big topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It came into my mind as well, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me -- I think that's a fair comment, so let's begin with the question of arming.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did that take place, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because, you see, this dispatch was sent to the top leaders of Serbian origin in those particular towns, and they disposed of all the equipment in terms of weapons in those towns, both to the active-duty police and reserve police, and I'm talking about Sokolac, Bijeljina, Gorazde, and other towns, and Banja Luka, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if you would allow me just one question. You now mentioned Bijeljina as well, where in a prior --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- part of your testimony, when reading to whom this was addressed, you -- I think you left out Bijeljina, because it was stricken through, or at least it seems to be. Could you tell us whether it was also sent to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read the name of Bijeljina on the front page, but it doesn't indicate that it was sent here. However, I know that the first policeman in Bijeljina was a Serb. His name was Miodrag Jesuric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is that also the name you decipher on the first page of this document? Because it's illegible in the translation. Mr. Mandic, that's the name you read also, Jesuric, on the front page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jesuric was his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as far as you remember, was it sent to Bijeljina as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was. I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Honours, and his name is Predrag Jesuric, not Miodrag.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct. His name was Predrag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tomic, I think you added something to the testimony which is not -- first of all, you make a correction on something I have not heard or seen. I didn't see any Miodrag. And so, therefore, there was no need for a correction. I think we fairly discussed what your role would be, and that's not supplementing the evidence of Mr. Mandic. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me try to clarify that quickly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, do you know Mr. Jesuric's first name?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His first name is Predrag.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you said that the centre leaders, the regional centre leaders to whom you sent your letter on February 13th, disposed of weapons in response. What did you mean by "disposed of the weapons"? What did they do with weapons in response to your February 13th letter?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each centre, apart from their regular stockpile of weapons, they had rifles that belonged to the reserve police force. So they disposed of this particular stockpiles of weapons, and each security centre in each major town kept these weapons in their depots.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did they do so so those weapons would be available to the Serbian MUP once it split from the joint MUP, and not to the members of a remaining Muslim MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to that, did you or Mr. Stanisic or others participate in the delivery or dissemination of weapons to Serbian police stations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For many years before that, the weapons were kept for many years in the depots for the purpose of the reserve police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you to look at another exhibit, if I may, then, and that would be 0121-5571.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this exhibit, P417, is an interview published in Slobodna Bosna of April 10th, 1998. Excuse me. In Oslobodjenje, in April of 1998, with you. The interviewer was Jelena Stamenkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is Slobodna Bosna, we understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at the original, Mr. Tieger, you'll see it says Slobodna Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in the first part of the article, Mr. Mandic, you give some of your background, describing the fact that you'd been involved with the MUP since the age of 15 and talking about some of your history and some of the events leading up to tensions in the MUP. And then the next question is: In what ways did you help the Serbian side? And your answer in that article is: "I gave them or put at their disposal official cars. I recruited and admitted to the police force those Serbs proposed by Radovan Karadzic and Ranko Dukic, but I also gave them some material means and communications equipment. We would even deliver weapons to Serbian police stations, for example, in Pale, Sokolac, et cetera. We grabbed and shared out as much as was needed."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a meeting in Krtelji, I think it took place on the 3rd of April, 1992, which was attended by the Croatian, Muslim, and Serbian leaders, the joint leadership of MUP, and that is when the special unit was divided, and the Serbian part of the special unit, 35 men, headed by Milenko Karisik went to Rakovica [phoen], a part of the company Upi at the time, and it was agreed that the Serbian part of the police would go to Vrace, to the old special police barracks and that a new special police base, Krtelji, would be placed at the disposal of the Croats and Muslims who remained behind. On the night between Saturday and Sunday, that is, between the 4th and the 5th April, we went to Vrace, where an armed conflict broke out between the reserve police members, composed of Muslims, and the Serbian special police forces, and as a result, two Serbian policemen, special policemen, were killed. Their names were Pupic and Lopatic, and the other two were wounded. There were no casualties on the Muslim side. That is when we entered the school building in Vrace and the old special police base. Concerning the recruitment of personnel and with the consent of Rajko Dukic and Karadzic, each municipality, the town and region, proposed three members each from their own ethnic groups. The recruitment commission, Dukic and Karadzic, coordinated views with us and we had chosen the best people to be admitted into our ranks. So if in a town the chief was a Muslim, the police commander would be a Serb, and the CID chief would be a Croat, or vice versa: If the chief of the police was a Croat, the commander was a Muslim and the CID chief would be a Serb. This referred exclusively to leadership in certain police stations and in certain security services centres that at the time were five in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me return, if I may, to the specific question of arming, however. I had asked you whether or not part of the preparation for separating the joint MUP was the arming of Serb police or certain Serb police stations, and in the article in Slobodna Bosna -- so is the -- let me ask it more directly. Is the answer yes, part of the preparation did include arming of Serb police and Serb police stations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in addition, I had asked you earlier, as part of a compound question, whether or not the beginnings of terminations of Muslims from police stations began before the actual or final separation of the joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A single Muslim [as interpreted], as far as I know, was dismissed between the separation of the MUP and before I sent the dispatch to that effect. And I repeat: The moment the ethnic or nationalist parties won made it more difficult to maintain the balance of relationships within the MUP, reflecting the national, ethnic composition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because we had a surplus of the Serbs in the MUP. And the Serbs who were dismissed, not Muslims, at least not until I sent this dispatch or this telegram instructing the division of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's going to be a fairly obvious correction, I think, when anybody is reading the transcript, but plainly, the word "not" should have been at the very -- or was at the very beginning of that answer, and needs to be there on the transcript at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mandic, did you say not a single Muslim, as far as you know, was dismissed between the separation of the MUP and before you sent the dispatch to that effect? Yes. May I just ask you for your attention --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the MUP headquarters, as far as I know, not a single Muslim was dismissed from any police station. Whether there were any isolated cases, I cannot say. It may have happened in other municipalities, but I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I ask you whether my impression is right that you are asking several times what happened after this dispatch was sent and that Mr. Mandic elaborates on what happened before that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Perhaps I've been unclear. This -- I think Mr. Mandic correctly understood my intention to ask him about any terminations before the dispatch was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's my misunderstanding. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me clarify that, and my apologies for really confusing the issue. The term "dispatch" is one that we'll hear in relation to a couple of documents. With reference to the February 13th letter that Mr. Mandic sent, you are correct, and I think Mr. Mandic also understood that it was correct, that I was referring to events after that. That's true. And -- but I was referring to events after that February 13th letter, but before the final separation of the unified MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear to me now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, with regard to individual cases in which Muslims were dismissed from police stations, let me ask you if you recall events in Sokolac that may have been precipitated by Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that before the final separation of the MUP, Mr. Cvijetic had dismissed all Muslim staff, and at our joint meeting, we passed a decision to suspend this police station, that it be excluded from financing and also from the rest of the BH MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Muslims had been dismissed and ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was because he dismissed the Muslim employees at his own will. And I think that was the only one and the first case of that nature, did that without the knowledge or the consent from anyone in the MUP, both the Serbian or other officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And despite the decision by the leadership of the joint MUP in response to the actions of Mr. Cvijetic, did you, in conjunction with Mr. Karadzic, take steps to ensure that the police force in Sokolac, led by Mr. Cvijetic, would continue to receive pay?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, that anything of that nature was taken. Mico Stanisic was in charge of these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that connection, then, Mr. Mandic, let me direct your attention to two documents that might assist. The first is a small portion of the 36th Assembly session of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be Exhibit P418.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note that there's an English translation of this document that I think we need to improve upon by separating from the rest of the document. I apologise for that. And we will take steps as soon as possible to rectify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from that, Mr. Tieger, could the logistics be improved as well? Because usually when you indicate that a new document will be presented to a witness, it's still on your desk, then it has to travel all around the courtroom. If we could just go one document ahead, so that would save a lot of time. So that, for example, now the next -- that P419 would already be put at the disposal of Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure we can remedy that at this session. We'll do so at the first opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you be so kind as to provide the ERN number for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'm directing your attention to a short excerpt from that session, during which you speak and say to the members of the Assembly: "It's true, gentlemen. Vito and Delimustafic wanted to put me in gaol and you know why: Because together with Stanisic I took 560 Hecklers to Romanija and divided them between Sokolac, Rogatica, Han Pijesak, and Pale; and because when Zoran Cvijetic was commander of the public security station in Sokolac three months before the war, I drove all the Muslims out of the station and suspended them and Vito and Alija forbade me to pay their pensions and I paid them out of a special fund for fuel and pay." And let me also direct your attention to another exhibit referring to the same events, and that's ETV 000-243600.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I wonder if Mr. Tieger could just remind us or inform us. The 36th Assembly, I'm afraid I simply don't remember the date of that. And the particular document that was put to the witness a moment ago, P418, just says "Assembly of Republika Srpska, 1992 to 1995." So it's taken from a more compendious document. I just wonder if we could have the date, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll have to retrieve that, Your Honour. I don't know the precise date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could proceed, and once the date has been found, you'll tell us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P419 is an interview with you by a gentleman named Risto Djogo on a programme called "My Guest is Truth." And if I could direct your attention to your comments that appear at approximately about 25 per cent into the interview but at a portion marked 3210. You can see along the side that there are markings representing the length of the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're hopelessly confused. First of all, we don't see the reference; and secondly, this doesn't seem to be an interview with this gentleman at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What ERN number do you have in front of you you're referring to, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The ERN number of the document I'm referring to, Your Honour, is ET V000-2436001725.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have a different document, I'm afraid. We have ERN, and then V000 and then 2436, but nothing more. So there seems to be some confusion. Would you perhaps show your document, just to compare whether it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please switch -- I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I apologise. It's the document, the format looked the same, and my document indicates transcript of the broadcast "My Guest is Truth" with Momcilo Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what this document says. And we noticed that a portion marked 3210 does not appear in the original B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems that there are three documents, we believe, with the first lot of numbers, but then there's a suffix of further numbers which is where the discrepancy has emerged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I can see where the problem arose. The only issue is how to resolve it effectively here. My suggestion would be as follows, Your Honour. If it would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be put on the ELMO so that we -- is there a possibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you -- the document Mr. Tieger is using at this moment should be put on the ELMO. Mr. Tieger, would you -- are you referring only to that part at 1832 or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The part depicted on screen now is simply the first page, indicating the introduction to the broadcast, and I would direct the witness's attention to a portion on page 5 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's the portion that is highlighted toward the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you perhaps would read it slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will. That portion of the interview during which you're speaking, Mr. Mandic, states: "However, at the time, I had a special cash register, as the head of one of the Ministry departments, and since Zoran Cvijetic, God rest his soul, was the head of police in Sokolac, who jumped before all of us and didn't exactly behave by the agreed policy, he fired all employees of Muslim nationality before everybody else did, and as a result, the police station in Sokolac was suspended. Of course, people had to receive their salaries, to buy fuel and everything else, because they didn't have means to live and work. In the agreement with Mico Stanisic, he was already Serbian minister of Serbian MUP, but with the knowledge of Radovan Karadzic, I transferred the means from that cash register to Sokolac. That was to cover the salaries, the fuel, and all that. That was very risky move which I hid in the paperwork and decisions, saying that some of it went to Banja Luka, some of it to Medici, some on different places. And that was the way we kept this station going for two months."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, having an opportunity to hear again your comments from the 36th Assembly session and your remarks during the interview with Mr. Djogo, does that refresh your memory about your response to the suspension of the Sokolac police department?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't exactly like that. In the special treasury or cash register, I had two or three thousand German marks at the time, and that certainly wasn't enough to cater to the salaries and expenses of the SUP Sokolac. But the media kept stressing the role and importance of individuals, so I mentioned this. But quite certainly, these people from Sokolac received fuel from somewhere else, and I think their salaries too, from the Sokolac SUP. And this can be checked out. If you look at the records of the MUP, you will be able to see how many months this was and how many months my special cash register had to cater to. I think this was more media publicity than actually what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me see if I can parse that out somewhat. Of course, you've already indicated that the Sokolac SUP was suspended, and why. Is it correct that you took some steps in response to that to ensure that this now exclusively Serbian police force would be kept going?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by way of money. I didn't give any money, because in my cash register I had a very small amount of money; negligible, in fact, which was not enough for the employees. And as I said, this was more for the purposes of the media, for publicity and the role -- to increase my role in all this. Now, as far as fuel is concerned, I think that during that time some fuel was taken away from the Sokolac police station and that they used that fuel for their own vehicles. That's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were efforts being made to keep the Sokolac SUP going and to pay the Serbian police and at least do ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And to the extent you could, I take it you supported that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, we've referred --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I ask Mr. Mandic. Mr. Mandic, you say this was -- you didn't pay -- it was publicity, but in the Assembly of the Republika Srpska that was just read to you, I think, you said: I paid them out of a special fund for fuel and pay. That's how to reconcile that you said that you did not pay and what you said in the Assembly of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. In the Assembly there was a verbal duel between myself and Biljana Plavsic. We clashed, because our views diverged on certain issues. And at one point she called for my dismissal. And in my verbal duel with Mrs. Plavsic, I stressed that at one point in time I had helped the Sokolac police station in material terms and in terms of fuel. However, as far as this material assistance was concerned, there was none, because my special cash register or treasury as the head, was very small, negligible, as I said. I only had two or three thousand marks and some dinars, which was negligible and a very small amount, which couldn't help anybody. It certainly couldn't help the MUP employees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But do I understand that you spent money not to pay employees but to pay fuel for Sokolac? Or did you not at all pay? So were you not telling the truth in the Assembly of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're defending yourself, your position, you're saying you did pay --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness's answer "correct" came following a fairly composite question from Your Honour. It's very difficult to see what he's affirming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I'll clarify. Mr. Mandic, when you said in the Assembly of Republika Srpska: "I paid them out of a special fund," did you pay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, you've referred on more than one occasion to the final splitting of the MUP. Let me direct your attention, then, to Prosecution's next in order, 0049-0125.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as the previous document is concerned, is that now the one that is going to be 419, scrapping the original, incorrect one? And then are we go going to get --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It certainly will not, because it will add to the confusion. I take it, Mr. Tieger, you will distribute immediately after the break a document in which the text appears that you just read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct and that's what I understood Mr. Stewart's question to be whether that distributed document correcting reflecting the interview to which we were referring will now become 419.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That seems logical to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was my question and the answer I'm a hundred per cent happy with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next exhibit will be P420.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we at some point, if Mr. Tieger could just possibly take the opportunity of checking it or having it checked over the break, if we could, please, have the dates of that 36th Assembly. We could, I suppose, check that as well, but Mr. Tieger, I believe, is going to do that. And then also the date of that programme, "My Guest is Truth," that was being referred to a few minutes ago. That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, Mr. Tieger, is this something you could -- this subject you could finish within five minutes? If not, I would suggest that we'll continue after the break and give Mr. Stewart an opportunity to explain in the five minutes he asked for the procedural issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It seems like a perfectly appropriate time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I heard you saying that this was a perfectly appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we'll have a break for approximately a half-hour for you. Madam Usher will lead you out of the courtroom. We'll first deal with a procedural matter and then we'd like to see you back after the break. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the matter relates to the material which was supplied direct by Mr. Krajisnik to the Trial Chamber, and the reason why I said I believed I could be fairly short is because I don't wish to discuss the content of that particular material at all. Of course the Trial Chamber, not in much of a position to discuss the content because in response to my question you specifically have not looked at it. But I should say, Your Honour, apart from a glance, neither have I, at the moment. I know it relates to the witness Mr. Bjelobrk, and I know the broad nature although I haven't myself opened the compact disk. But the point of principle is this, Your Honour, that occasional opportunities for Mr. Krajisnik to communicate direct in court here to the Tribunal are an exception to the general position that the conduct of the case is in the hands of his counsel. When from time to time for practical convenience any sort of material is communicated by the parties directly to the Trial Chamber, and it is -- as between Prosecution and Defence, of course, we offer each other the correct courtesy of providing copies for each other, because there shouldn't be unilateral or secret, as it were, communications with the Trial Chamber. So that procedure is followed without any problem at all. And of course, anything coming from Mr. Krajisnik, we would never wish to disguise, nor should we disguise from the Prosecution that that has arrived. And in a sense it's not confidential, either, because whatever Mr. Krajisnik's intentions if material for practical convenience is transmitted behind the scenes for the Trial Chamber, it still should be public because it's only a practical substitute for what in principle should be conveyed in open court. So that's the, if you like, the underlying analysis, we would say, of the position. However it comes to this, Your Honour, that I make it clear, and it's consistent with the position that we have adopted as counsel before: That we do not wish Mr. Krajisnik to make such communications to the Trial Chamber. We wish, as his counsel, to have the conduct of the case, as is the correct principle, the correct approach; as enshrined as it happens both in the conduct code of conduct applicable specifically to this Tribunal and to the very similar codes of conduct applicable to me as a member of the bar of England and Wales, and Ms. Loukas as the members of the bar of New South Wales. We do wish to do that. And therefore, our request, Your Honour, is that, subject I suppose always to very specific, very exceptional situations on which I would wish always to have the opportunity, please, of making submissions, comparable to the situation where Mr. Krajisnik wishes to address the Tribunal directly here in open court, we would ask that the Trial Chamber simply does not receive and is not willing to receive such direct communications from Mr. Krajisnik and simply returns them, either to Mr. Krajisnik or to us, as his counsel. But one way or another, that such material is simply returned and it is made clear to Mr. Krajisnik that unless some specific advance application is made by him to have some direct communication, sidestepping, as it were, his counsel, that any such communication should come through us. Your Honour, that is our submission. I can elaborate as necessary, but it doesn't really allow much elaboration. That is our -- I say request, but it is a submission and we do say it's correct in principle and it is consistent with our having the conduct of Mr. Krajisnik's case. And we of course submit it because we -- our submission and our view, and we can express a view here as counsel, is that that is in fact in Mr. Krajisnik's interests. We may have a conflict of view, Mr. Krajisnik and we as his counsel, but we as his counsel do not see it as a conflict of interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, may I first ask you whether you being aware of material sent directly to the Chamber, whether you discussed the matter with Mr. Krajisnik and whether this -- what would have been the result of this discussion. I can imagine that you would say it's a mistake, I'll ask it back or I'll first give it to you and ask the Judges not to look at it. There are various possibilities. But did you discuss it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't know anything about it until it had already been received by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. But after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Krajisnik knows my views on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He's waving his hand, Your Honour, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- and wishes to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course. Of course, the usual -- usually it's counsel who addresses the Chamber, but under these specific circumstances, I'll not ignore the waving hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. I'm not inviting you either in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, would you like to address the Chamber, in view of the material you sent?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for allowing me to address you. I have to say that I am taken by surprise by what counsel has just said. It was following your instructions that I sent my lawyers the documentation that I had sent to you, and they were stenographic notes. In order to assist you and for you to be able to focus on the critical elements in the stenographic notes, I put on the CD parts of the stenographic notes which had to do with the relevant issues linked to Mr. Bjelobrk, in order to justify the reason for which I wanted to highlight Mr. Bjelobrk and other important witnesses whom I wished to examine additionally, and that was my aim in doing that. But I did supply Mr. Stewart with all the documentation, and it was up to him to send those stenographic notes on to you, which I assume he did. But in my request, and I should like to ask you to do this now as well, I should like to have relevant witnesses such as the one we have here today to be allowed to ask them additional questions, because I am quite convinced that this witness has mixed up the events with the relevant times and that very often, unconsciously, he is in fact not telling the truth because of that. So that was my purpose with Mr. Bjelobrk and other witnesses too. Therefore, Your Honour, let me repeat this in an open session: I have very good and skilful lawyers, and that is my opinion of Mr. Stewart. But I am very dissatisfied with the manner in which the defence case is being conducted, because they are not ready for a defence case and they don't understand certain matters because they don't have enough time to delve into them. And, unfortunately, our communication has been rather poor. That is why in order to assist the Trial Chamber, and in order to assist the Defence case generally, to help him, and to help myself, and to help you have the proceedings evolve as well as possible. So I should now like to ask you this -- and I discussed this witness, today's witness, with Mr. Stewart. I think we have managed to clarify many matters. And if he does succeed in getting through the important points and examine the witness on the important points, then I won't ask you to allow me to ask the witness additional questions. Now, everything he said about me is true but needs explanation, because it is in a different light that they should be seen. I would like to be allowed to ask additional questions of witnesses who mention me, not the other witnesses, and Ms. Loukas is doing that very well herself. She is conducting the cross-examination very well. But when it comes to witnesses of this kind, whom I knew, could you please make an exception and allow me to ask additional questions. If I can't do so in this way and be allowed to do so in this way, then I shall have to do it in a different manner. But let me say that I don't wish to do so, because I am very satisfied with the way this trial is being conducted and I should like to assist the Trial Chamber. I'm very happy to see when you ask witnesses questions yourself, because it is always your intention to ascertain the truth. So I thank you for that and that is what I had to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. First of all, we have two issues now. The first issue is the material sent to the Judges, and I think Mr. Krajisnik added a matter which is, by way of exception, to allow him to put questions to this witness. I would say the second issue we'll not give any decision now because there are still a lot of uncertainties about when this witness will be cross-examined. So, therefore, I'd rather not going into that area. I also now do understand, Mr. Krajisnik, that you, where - I'm now working from my memory - where I said that in stenographic notes could give a more precise picture of certain meetings, that of course those stenographic notes might assist the Chamber. And I think then the misunderstanding is only about how to introduce such matters. From my experience as defence counsel, I can tell you that defence counsel, whatever happens, and even if they would totally agree that it would be helpful to have such precise and detailed information available to a Trial Chamber, that defence counsel always want to see it first. Therefore, I think we are mainly talking about which procedure to follow. I do understand that you prepared the stenographic notes in such a way that they are accessible for everyone who wants to read them. Would you mind if we would -- it's about Mr. Bjelobrk, which is not something that's dealing with today or tomorrow. Would you mind if we return it to you, if you send it to Mr. Stewart, that Mr. Stewart looks at it. If there's any hesitation whatsoever -- in timing, in content, in whatever -- if he has any hesitation to send it to the Chamber, that you would discuss that; and that if you agree on sending it to the Trial Chamber, then of course we would need to find the proper procedural way of introducing it and to have it in evidence. That's a technical aspect, on which I certainly think Mr. Stewart could find the appropriate ways of doing that. Would that be a solution for you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing against that. And it was not my intention to make a problem here, and I completely share your opinion that the best thing is when one has a good cooperation with one's lawyer. Because I have a good lawyer. I don't have a bad lawyer. If I did, I would say it loud and clear here. But I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I take it that this resolved this matter. And let's not give rulings in general terms, because it seems to be a misunderstanding where Mr. Krajisnik only wanted to assist the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm perfectly happy that we have resolved this particular matter, and the wider, more general principles and questions, I think Your Honour is suggesting and I would, with respect, completely agree that those should be left for another day, another time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps they might never come up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can live in hope, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we'll return the material to you, and we do understood that there's a fair chance sooner or later in whatever form we'll receive it anyhow and of course the Prosecution will be aware of it as well. And we now adjourn until five minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I just say, Your Honour, that Your Honour is 100 per cent right, call us old fashioned, but yes as Defence counsel we really, really do like to see material first. Yes, Your Honour is absolutely right about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We adjourn until five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber now received a copy of P419, the new one. "My Guest is Truth." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And in that connection, there was a question about the date of that interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is shown on the cover page of the document as July, August 1994. I can also indicate at this time that the date of the 36th Assembly session was 30 December 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And lastly, Your Honour, I would indicate that we provided lined versions of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: B/C/S originals, yes. Mr. Stewart, will we receive a B/C/S copy of P419 soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, Your Honour is addressing or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to be clear, Your Honour, because I wouldn't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I see P419 is only in English at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's not available at the moment, Your Honour. We'll have it at the first opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed. Just in order to save paper, is it of any use to keep the old P419, which then will reappear under another number, or is it better to give rid of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think we'll see it again in this examination again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, of course, the witness should be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Tieger very helpfully indicated that we would be provided with a lined version of the B/C/S. We're now totally at a loss as to what it is we're being provided with a lined version of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I took it that it was from the -- I take it from the interviews with Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you say the interviews. It would be the March interview. The only one available in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, please be seated. Mr. Tieger will resume his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, just before the recess, I think you had been provided with Prosecution's Exhibit 420, which is a document dated March 31st, 1992 and bears your signature as deputy minister of the interior. And just for clarification, as an initial matter, Mr. Mandic, although the English translation says "deputy minister of the interior," is it correct that your position with the joint MUP at that time, that is, on March 31st, 1992, was assistant minister in charge of crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, more substantively, Mr. Mandic, is the document we're looking at now, P420, the directive to Serbian police officers in accordance with the decisions of the Assembly and the February 11th, 1992 meeting to split the joint MUP? Sorry, Mr. Mandic. Are you taking your time and reading the document or did you not understand the question?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for a question. I know the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. No. The question was whether or not you can confirm that this is the document that was sent to Bosnian Serb police officials and officers in accordance with the decision of the Assembly of the Serbian People and with the February 11th meeting to split up the joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, was the dissemination of this document effectively the start of the war in Bosnia? That is, did you, in effect, by sending this document, begin the conflict in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not an appropriate question. That's -- it's far beyond and far too general beyond any factual question which is appropriate to address to this witness. Questions must be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me refine it slightly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. Especially the phrase "start of the war" is too unclear, I would say. Well, I would say that you could give all kind of answers to that, depending on how you interpret these words, and there should be no confusion about the question itself. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, at the time you sent the document, did you realise or believe that the dissemination of this document would commence the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only acted in accordance to the decisions of the Serbian people which on the 27th of March, 1992, passed such a decision, and also the law on the interior. Since I was a high-ranking administration official, or actually, in terms of rank, the top official in the joint MUP, I was instructed by the newly appointed minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic, to send this kind of telegram, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, may I just interfere. I'd like you to carefully listen to the question, because from your answer, you explained why and on whose instructions you sent this document. The question, however, was whether you did realise or believe that the dissemination of the document would commence the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, he did -- I'm sorry. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would say that acting on instructions was the only thing you had in your mind, that's clear; but one does not exclude the other. Mr. Tieger did not specifically ask you on whose instructions you sent the document, but he asked you whether you believed this to have a certain effect or that it would bring about a certain result or would start a kind of development. I'd like you to focus especially on the question put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness does that, Your Honour, I apologise to be too hasty, because sometimes it's difficult to judge, Your Honour, before the -- well, I won't say that, Your Honour. But he did answer the question. He answered it very specifically. He then went on to add something, but he answered the question with the very first single word of his answer. And if that had stood, it was a complete answer to Mr. Tieger's question. He then added something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you would consider the following lines, where he starts: "No. Only -- I only." If that would be an explanation of his first answer, it still -- the question should be put to him again. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, irrespective of who gave you instructions to prepare and disseminate the document, did you understand at that time that the dissemination of that document would commence the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not think about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently come, or later come to understand that by the dissemination of that document, you and those who had instructed you to send it had started the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not clear why this witness's subsequent opinion, retrospectively, is part of his factual evidence before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the -- I think it's a predicate question which has a considerable relevance, Your Honour. The determination or the significance of this particular act or this particular document is of considerable importance to this case, and I think this is clearly a witness who can shed some light on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He's not a witness of opinion, Your Honour. He's not a witness of opinion. The fact that he may have subsequently formed some view has then really not nothing to do with the facts. If this is intended to elicit some factual evidence from the witness, then that should be done specifically rather than seeking opinion evidence from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure Your Honour has turned his microphone off at any point. It's only fair for -- we sometimes make that mistake, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was no microphone open.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why it is, then, through the ether, we were managing to hear quite a bit of what Your Honours were saying. It's -- I think it's only fair to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for drawing our attention to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am aware that we have some difficulties now and then, but there's nothing really scandalous about what the Judges exchanged. The objection is sustained. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'd like to direct your attention to Prosecution's next exhibit in order. I don't know if the registrar has it at this point. It's L009-7976.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, just to avoid whatever confusion: Your number you gave is L009-7976. What we have in front of us now is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to guess you have 0303.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then 1202.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. Well, that is the -- I tried to signal that the exhibit to which I was turning, in light of the responses and the Court's ruling, might be different from the one that the registrar had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But I encourage the Court to hang on to 0303.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Which is P421 now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what was supposed to become P421, I do understand will most likely be P422.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P421 is a document dated March 21st, 1992 [sic], bearing the signature of the Minister of the Interior, Alija Delimustafic. And Mr. Delimustafic was your direct superior; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I see in the transcript "document dated March 21st, 1992." I take it it should be 31st.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Definitely the 31st, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mandic. Mr. Delimustafic was your direct superior, as the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in this document, he expresses his reaction to the dispatch that we just looked at and which you sent; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And among other things, Mr. Delimustafic expresses the belief that the majority of MUP employees want to work in a unified or united MUP and that they find any segregation, particularly on a national basis, difficult, and he urges MUP employees not to allow anyone to separate them from their colleagues; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me also ask you, then, to direct your attention to Prosecution's next in order, which is ET 0210-0215.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P422 is an issue from 1 April 1992 of Oslobodjenje that directs its attention to the division of the MUP announced yesterday, or as it says at the beginning of the article, the division of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Mr. Mandic, let me ask you first of all if you have that article from Oslobodjenje in front of you. Take a moment, then, to orient yourself to it. This issue devotes considerable attention to the events of the previous day and to the division of the MUP, as you can see. We've already examined the reaction of the minister of the interior to the dispatch that you sent. On page 2 of the English translation, we see a portion of that issue entitled "MUP union organising a public protest. No to the divisions." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that reflects, does it not, the response of the independent union of the persons employed at the Ministry of Internal Affairs, which stated in part: "Shall we look at each other as targets? Shall we forget the decades of work while protecting each others' back? Shall we provoke the beginning of the war by dividing the war that will take our loved ones?" And the article goes on to note that certain members of the union of Serbian nationality did not support an undivided MUP and would be expressing that view as well. Was the reaction in Oslobodjenje, the reaction of the independent union of employees of the MUP, part of the immediate response to the dispatch that you sent instructing the division of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And similarly, in connection with that, I'd like to ask you to look at Prosecution's next in order, ET SA 04-0273.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P423 is a document sent to, as you can see, many levels of the joint MUP, from the public security station in Zvornik. And it's signed by the Zvornik public security station chief and the leaders of its organisational units. Now, that document also expresses a reaction specifically to the fax that was sent by you on March 31st, as well as the fax that was sent by Minister of Interior Delimustafic in response; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it expresses the view that the -- that all workers of the Zvornik public security station are in favour of unity in the MUP and therefore against any divisions on an ethnic basis, and also urges urgent measures in the joint MUP to clear up inter-ethnic relations in the leadership of the MUP and to stop the manipulation of employees because this is very dangerous at this time and could lead to inter-ethnic conflicts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
