utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, having reviewed those documents -- the response from the public security station officials in Zvornik; who expressed their concern that division of the MUP would lead to inter-ethnic conflict; the position of the union of MUP employees that dividing the MUP would be the beginning of a war, a war that would take the lives of their loved ones; the response of Mr. Delimustafic -- does that refresh your recollection at all on your awareness of the impact that dividing the MUP would have on Bosnia and Herzegovina and the relative likelihood that it would produce an inter-ethnic conflict?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in fact, Mr. Mandic, did you later acknowledge that by sending the fax on March 31st, in response to instructions as you've indicated, that you and Mr. Stanisic effectively began the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I turn, Your Honour, now to 0303-1202.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the one that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- was prematurely distributed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P424 is an interview with you by Ekstra Magazin, conducted by Radmila Zigic. As you can see from the caption under the photograph, "I hope to be the first and last ambassador in my own state," it was conducted at the time when you were director or the chief of the bureau in Belgrade in 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it possible to be more specific than that in putting the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you have any further details?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I only have a contextual date for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, that would be correct, would it not, that the interview was conducted at a time when you were director of the bureau? If you would look at both the caption under the photograph, and I would turn your attention to about the fourth question: "Can your office of director of the bureau be considered an ambassadorial post, as it is often popularly designated?" I believe the questions are underlined.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I directed your attention to that particular question simply to ask you if -- to confirm that the interview took place at a time when you were the director of the bureau in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was in 1993 and 1994; is that right? I realise that's only -- that's a broad range.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the time when I was the director of the bureau.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it isn't very satisfactory to have such a broad range in relation to a document which is, after all, in a published organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you're invited to give further details as soon as possible on the date of publication of the Ekstra Magazin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will advise the Court at the earliest opportunity if we could advise of the date or of the reasons why not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, we were interested to have the date. I take it it must be somewhere. Of course if you have no date, of course we'd like to be informed why not. But yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'd like to direct your attention to a portion of that interview which occurs late in the interview, and if you'll turn to the -- about the fifth question from the last one. That question begins: Biljana Plavsic is not the only person who got her relatives out. First of all, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in the course of your answer to that question, you say the following: "The fact that some see me as Slobodan's man is a result of the fact that Mico Stanisic and I are friends. Mico Stanisic and I started the war in Bosnia. We separated the Serbian part of the MUP, created the MUP, and set out to Vrace. We were supposed to be shot by firing-squad that evening." And then you go on to compare yourself to others who did not engage in similar actions and while labels are being stuck on you. Mr. Mandic, does that refresh your recollection about subsequently acknowledging that the splitting of the MUP commenced the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Maybe it's just me here. Mr. Tieger in his question started with a quotation, "the fact that some see me as Slobodan's man is a result of the fact that Mico Stanisic and I are friends. Mico Stanisic and I started the war." I can see Mico Stanisic and I started the war in the bold passage, but I can't see immediately before that the reference to "some see me as" -- "the fact that some see me as Slobodan's man." I'm just not seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The bold passage is a paraphrase of the actual text that appears before that. So if you look to the unbolded text, immediately below that you'll see the passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the original you'll see highlighted portions. It's clear to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I see now. Well, yes. What a strange way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you'll repeat your question to the witness, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, does that refresh your recollection about subsequently acknowledging that the splitting of the MUP commenced the conflict in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The division of the MUP did not precipitate the war in Bosnia. I'll quote the example of Bijeljina, where inter-ethnic clashes started well before the 31st of March. The clashes in Herzegovina began much before the 31st of March, and that applied to Mosor as well. That is before the dispatch. Also, the Serbian policemen were killed in the SUP of Novo Sarajevo and in the area of Capljina. Therefore, there were armed incidents before. One of the most prominent took place in Bijeljina, when Biljana Plavsic and other top officials of Bosnia-Herzegovina went to meet Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, where armed conflict broke out when the paramilitary forces captured that town. And that was at least one month before the division of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you indicated a couple of times in response to questions about the splitting of the unified MUP into ethnic divisions that you were acting in accordance with instructions that you were given; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is that something you've consistently maintained as well, that is, that your act was not your -- not your sole initiative, but that you were acting at the behest of your superiors?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that connection, can I ask you to turn to another portion of the article. That would be the fifth question from the beginning of the article in P424.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, have you finished with this portion of the interview? Because I would have an additional question then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the interview states that you've said "Mico Stanisic and I started the war in Bosnia," and then, in the following lines, it says how you separated the Serbian part of the MUP, that you created the MUP, et cetera. If you did not start the war, if the war was not started by the separation of the Serbian part of the MUP, not by the creation of the MUP but by other events, how did you then start the war, as the interview says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that was a free interpretation by the journalist. I cannot recall exactly what I said 12 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does this mean that you say that you did not say to the journalist that you started the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember what I said to the journalist 12 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to make an observation about this question unusually in the absence of the witness, about this particular -- not specifically Your Honour's question, in fact, but the -- this whole passage in the interview. And I would, if I may, I would particularly like to make that in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mandic, could you please follow the usher and leave the courtroom for a second. Mr. Stewart, would you find it appropriate, also in view of the role of counsel, that he remain here?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not troubled by the remaining presence of counsel on the basis that there is no communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He's instructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's this: It's really to raise a possibility, because I don't know the answer to this. But it does look as if it's distinctly possible -- this answer, as reported by the journalist in this interview, and I'm talking about page 4 of the English, the fact that "some see me as Slobodan's man is a result of the fact that Mico Stanisic and I are friends "and then the next bit, which is the critical passage: Mico Stanisic and I started the war in Bosnia; we separated the Serbian part of MUP; created the MUP and set out to Vrace; we were supposed to be shot by firing-squad that evening. That last bit does at least raise the possibility that what was happening here was not simply the witness saying this is my view -- and after all, it's a second-hand report by a journalist, anyway -- but that he was really reciting or reported by the journalist as saying, reciting what others were saying, and particularly "we were supposed to be shot by firing-squad." Is he saying that in his view we were supposed to be shot by firing-squad or that somebody else was saying they were supposed to be shot by firing-squad? So I hope I'm making myself clear. The underlying basis of this questioning may be flawed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be. We'll -- I do understand. Rightly you have drawn our attention to a possible interpretation of what this interview says and you also rightly have drawn our attention to the fact that, of course, this is not necessarily a literal reference to what he said, but cautions us. To act cautiously in this respect is something the Chamber fully understands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I take advantage of the fact the witness is out of the court to say something, that as Mr. Tieger explores once again this area of who gave instructions to whom, we don't appear yet in this bit of the evidence to have got into the realm of a justification for hostile witness, cross-examination-type questions. Our submission is that we are still in a mode, if I may put it that way, where the questions here should be put in as neutral and non-leading a form as possible, at least in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Court is asking me for a response to Mr. Stewart's suggestion that -- I'm not sure he's directing the Court's attention or my attention to any particular question --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I could, if it would help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tieger, Mr. Stewart is asking your attention that at least on some major points, there are no indications at this moment that the need to keep the witness on the track you had in mind has become clear, and therefore you should refrain from leading. And specifically, Mr. Stewart referred to the issue of instructions received by the witness. I just want to know whether you take his suggestion or that you say: No, the basis for what he -- the basis and the course of the examination is such that you would disagree with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I do, Your Honour. And I understand the Court's instructions, and I understood from the way the examination had been proceeding that the Court was reasonably satisfied that the examination was proceeding in a fair manner, which is certainly my intention. To the extent that there is any inadvertent deviation from that, I will of course attempt to correct it. But I am attempting to direct the witness's attention to issues that need to be discussed, but not in any particular manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I do understand that Mr. Stewart says that if there's no clear indication that there's any need to lead the witness, that at least you should start in a non-leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I thought I had been, and where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No. I think it was just in order to avoid any problems in the near future.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It might help if I'm a little bit specific there, Your Honour. Mr. Tieger was about, perhaps in his mind, is about to put to the witness the fifth question in this interview, and what I'm saying is that it's not appropriate for him at this point to put that fifth question and the answer to that fifth question to the witness, because it's clearly designed to lead the witness into the answer to the question which Mr. Tieger was asking him a short while ago, as to where he got his instructions in relation to the splitting of the MUP. So that's the specific point. In general, the way that cross-examination -- examinations, slip of the tongue -- the way that examinations proceed fairly is by counsel asking questions, counsel on the other side objecting as appropriate and the Trial Chamber making appropriate rulings. That's how we achieve fairness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the point is clear now. Mr. Tieger, unless you would have any further comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have any further comment, Your Honour. I think the way -- and I'm going to say again. I think the way the examination is proceeding is entirely fair. I disagree with counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll continue, then. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom. I would have one or two more questions to the witness on the issue raised before Mr. Stewart intervened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Mandic. Did you read the interview as published at the time it was published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember this interview at all, to be quite frank, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I had just directed your attention to the fifth question that appears in the article, and that question is directed to your reaction to the political conflict and severance of relations between Republika Srpska and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And your first sentence in response is: "As a man, I am very devoted to both Slobodan Milosevic and to Radovan Karadzic. With Karadzic and Krajisnik, I began the war in Sarajevo and now when I am sitting here and watching what happened, I find justification for the Serbian leadership of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is exactly the question to which I was specifically objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's the whole problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. Let me just ask you -- Mr. Mandic, do you speak any English? Do you understand any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to ask you again to leave the courtroom for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, what would be your question? I mean, if your question would be: Is this what you said to a reporter? Then it's fair to put it to him, to this witness. If, however, your question would be: Is this the way you personally took the political conflict and the severance of the relations, then of course you have whispered the answer in his near such a leading way, against which Mr. Stewart clearly objected in advance. Could I ask you what your question would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, I'm sorry if that was understood as an objection in advance to that particular question. Let me set the backdrop to this particular question so that the Court can understand it in its entirety and rule fairly. The witness had said on a number of occasions that the splitting of the MUP was in response to instructions from his superiors or from the leadership. And I asked him if that was a position he maintained, he had maintained consistently, and I believe he indicated yes. We've heard considerable evidence about who the leadership was. This is hardly coming as a surprise, and this is corroboration of -- or not, depending on what the witness answers -- of just that. I accept fully that we're trying to proceed in a manner that is not leading, but I think the Court has to bear in mind that these are witnesses who are not proofed. Clearly in a proofing this kind of document would be presented to the witness he would be asked the relative significance in light of the overall information he gave. But now, in light of the objection that Mr. Stewart has been raising, we -- I think we've reintroduced into this process the sort of formalistic protocols that exist in jury systems whereby we ask a very general question in order to receive some kind of answer and move progressively toward the information that everybody knows is at the heart of the issue. I'm not trying to suggest answers to this witness, but I don't think that by presenting him with something that's been said before and asking him its relationship to those issues to which he has testified I'm doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think Mr. Stewart suggested that we'd start, at least, with an open question and then confront the witness with any answer he had given in an interview after that. I'll not give any general opinion of the Chamber on the trial techniques as developed in jury systems. It's not the time to do it. But we listen carefully to your objections to the use of that time-consuming way of examination of the witness. You're invited, Mr. Tieger, to put the question in a more general -- at least in a less leading way. The problem is that when you started reading, the Chamber, at least, didn't know what your question would be. Therefore, if you want to seek confirmation or denial of the words spoken to an interviewer, then of course you have to read it to the witness. But if you're trying to seek an answer to the question, a question that was put to the witness at that time by a journalist as well, then of course the proper way would be not to already read the answer to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be more, just for one moment, be more specific in the absence of the witness about what we submit the problem is. A few minutes ago, and it's now a few minutes ago, Mr. Tieger put the question to the witness about his getting instructions from the leadership in relation to the division of MUP. Now what he's doing, and we've seen this before, before he's inviting the witness to go further into that issue, he's putting very directly and specifically before the witness a piece of the interview where, surprise, surprise, one of the names that appears is Mr. Krajisnik. That's the point. Of course the Prosecution want to link all this to Mr. Krajisnik; that's what we're here. But the way it should not be done in these circumstances, unless we, through answers we get to the point where it is legitimate -- but the way it should not be done in the first place is by waving Mr. Krajisnik's name under the nose of the witness in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Maybe that does get to the heart of the issue, Your Honour. Because I think that's a completely misguided approach to this matter. To say that the Prosecution is linking Mr. Krajisnik is precisely the -- illustrates the fallacious nature of that argument. We're talking about an article, we talked about a portion of it. Now -- an interview with this witness. Now I turn to another portion of the interview in which Mr. Krajisnik is linked to those particular acts. Why it's necessary to go through some -- I mean, with all respect, relatively formalistic approach which ignores the fact that this witness has identified who the leadership was in the course of this testimony; has said that he acted at the behest of the leadership in dividing the MUP; and now I turn to a portion of the interview that we're looking at at the time to direct his attention to it, that that is somehow the Prosecution linking Mr. Krajisnik rather than the exhibit itself or the witness himself, is false.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps the best course, Your Honour, would be for Mr. Tieger, then, to indicate, in the absence of the witness now, very specifically what his question is going to be. Having put this piece of the interview under the nose of the witness, what are the questions that are then going to follow? Because that will enable the Trial Chamber, and of course as it happens the Defence, the basis of any submissions, to see what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll first ask Mr. Tieger. I have to go back and return to exactly -- I do remember that the witness told us about the positions and the leadership. Was there a specific indication that these instructions to distribute this -- he said he acted on the instruction. Was Mr. Krajisnik specifically mentioned in that context?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik -- I don't think the word "Krajisnik" came up. He referred to the Assembly; he referred to the February 11th meeting;, referred to the Council of Ministers, where Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik participated in the discussion and so on. So in that sense, certainly yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say implicitly yes. Then this would ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give a ruling, you're invited to say exactly what the question will be to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm only hesitating because I had intended to ask that question some time back and we've gone through a few permutations since. But essentially, Your Honour, I think it was going to be whether or not this was a reflection of his consistent position that the act of splitting the MUP was not at his initiative; it was done at the behest of his superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll ask the witness to come in again, and I might have a few questions for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just make one observation on that. In the terms in which the question has just been expressed, the further question arises why it need to be asked. Because the witness -- that's in a sense asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please refer us to the exact source.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "That the act of splitting the MUP was not at his initiative, it was done at the behest of his superiors. I'd also have to track back about five or ten minutes into the transcript to find that answer. Because -- but as I recall it, Mr. Tieger said something like: And this was the splitting. This was done on the instructions of your superiors or on the instruction of the leaders. And he said yes. So he has said that. So, so far as what Mr. Tieger's question is supposed to be about to be is concerned, that's already been dealt with. If Mr. Tieger is then seeking to be more specific in identifying not simply the fact that Mr. Mandic got his instructions from somewhere else, but from whom specifically he got those instructions, then we go right back to the very objection I'm making: the putting in front of him specific names and, surprise, surprise, one specific name, Mr. Krajisnik, for the purposes of that exercise. And the reference is page 51, line 9 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you're moving too far away from your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Page 51, lines 9 through to line 17, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to take the parties back to page 41, where the witness said: "I was instructed by the newly appointed Minister of the Interior, Mico Stanisic, to send this kind of telegram, and that's what I did." So the direct instructions, Mr. Tieger, were given by Stanisic. Of course, on the basis of what had been decided before, but Mr. Mandic was not present at that meeting where these decisions were taken, if I correctly understood his testimony. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, the Council of Ministers meeting or February 11th meeting? Mr. Mandic was not present, as I understand it, at the Council of Ministers meeting. He was present at the February 11th meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then he was instructed to ... Let's call the witness in again and see whether we can hear some evidence from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I would have a few questions for you. As far as the instructions are concerned to separate the Serbian MUP from the united MUP, did I understand correctly that this was a decision taken by the Council of Ministers, in which you were not present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The decision was made by the Assembly of the Serb People in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and at the Assembly was the minister -- the Council of Ministers. I was not a member of the Council of Ministers myself, so I was not there at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It was later discussed on the 11th of February; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 11th of February, yes. This was discussed. The meeting was held in Banja Luka, of the leaders of Serb ethnicity in the joint MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And some conclusions were made that were presented to me by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you have sent these instructions or the dispatch to the -- to some of the MUP officers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I sent the dispatch to all the SUPs in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and all their administrations and all the security centres. I was informed, and I informed those centres in turn, that the new minister of the interior was Mico Stanisic and that a Serbian MUP had been established and then conveyed the instructions that I received from Mico Stanisic as the new minister about the work of the new SUP, Serbian SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there unanimity among those who you ever met on this subject, whether there should be a separate Serbian MUP or whether, within to say Serbian circles, were there any opponents against this idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I acted pursuant to the decisions made by the Council of Ministers and the Assembly of the Serb People. But I can tell you, Your Honour, that afterwards there were both kinds of reactions. Some were for united MUP -- or rather, they were sorry that the MUPs were separating on an ethnic basis, whereas others said that was the right thing to do because you couldn't cooperate with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And at the higher levels was there unanimity or was there a similar difference of view? I mean, the levels higher up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do you mean the Serb cadre or the Bosnia-Herzegovinian cadre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Serb cadre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, mostly they agreed, and as far as the Serbs were concerned in the joint Ministry of the Interior. Perhaps there were a few dissensions, but very few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us who dissented? Do you have any names of those dissenting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of them was Vitomir Zepinic, who was the deputy MUP minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as far as you were aware of and in view of the answers you have given in respect of who were the Bosnian Serb leadership, was there any disagreement on this issue, to your knowledge, within the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do you mean within the MUP or in the political leadership?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Political leadership.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the political leadership, there was a unanimous opinion to create a Serb MUP, and I received instructions from the political leadership of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you earlier indicated that you understood by "Serbian leadership" to include Mr. Karadzic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Karadzic was the president of the party, but he wasn't in the official organs in Bosnia-Herzegovina until the start of the war. However, he was consulted at all levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I know that Your Honour was given an injunction only very rarely to intervene when the Bench is asking questions, but Your Honour, we do submit in this particular area Your Honour has given one name that would be a particular area where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not finished yet with that. Mr. Mandic, in order to avoid whatever confusion, would you repeat to us what you consider to be the political Bosnian Serb leadership. That would include -- perhaps you've said it already, but then I ask you to repeat it, or at least to give your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Our transcripts are not working. I don't know whether Your Honours have the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have the same problem. The problem is if we do not say any more word, then it will not restart. If only for that reason. It will take a minute or two, presumably, so I suggest that we wait for a minute or two. Mr. Mandic, we have some technical problems. Therefore, it will take a couple of minutes to have them resolved. The technicians need someone to say something in order to test whether the system is working again: I see on my screen that LiveNote is restarting. I think it works now again. Is that correct? Yes. Then, Mr. Mandic, you have had ample time to think about it's answer to my last question. I think you said before who you considered to be included in the leadership. Could you give us an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When I asked you whether there was unanimity among the Bosnian Serb leadership, you asked: Do you mean the political leadership? I said yes, I mean the political leadership. Could you just give us the names of those you would consider to -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Radovan Karadzic; Momcilo Krajisnik, MA; Professor Djeric; all the deputies in the Serb Assembly; and the minister of MUP, Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when you said they were unanimous in favour of the separation of the Serbian MUP, you would say you referred to this circle of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed, but we have got two minutes left. I don't know whether you wanted to enter a new subject or whether this would be an appropriate time to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think this is probably an appropriate time to break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break until ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, before the recess, we had looked at some documents that were issued in the aftermath of the March 31st fax that you sent, and I'd like you to look at one additional document, that is, ETP 004-4627.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, that's a document signed by Minister of Internal Affairs Delimustafic, to the security centres and the public security services and the secretariat of internal affairs Sarajevo. And is that the document reflecting your termination of employment at the MUP by Mr. Delimustafic and as a result of a decision by the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina government?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As the document indicates, the reasons for the decision was as listed in the last paragraph a serious breach of the rules of the service, illegal actions and criminal behaviour while in the service of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your testimony, you stated that the first position you assumed after the outbreak of the conflict for the Bosnian Serb Republic was the position of deputy minister of the Serbian MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mico Stanisic authorised me to stand in for him. So I acted as deputy minister of the interior in the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you issued directives and instructions as the deputy minister of the Serbian MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was deputy minister, and at that time I had my office in Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at Prosecution's next in order, that's 0305-4901.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, P426 is a document which bears the heading of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ministry of the Interior, dated 16 April 1992, and sent to Mr. Jesuric at the public security station Bijeljina, and bearing your name as deputy minister and a signature. Is it a document that you signed, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you were instructing or directing Mr. Jesuric to do in that document.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the law of the interior was drafted, that is to say, of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a mistake was made, stating that the headquarters was not in Bijeljina, and it was supposed to be Bijeljina, because of the infrastructure and equipment that was in Bijeljina, and that is why that was supposed to be the seat of the MUP. So this was a small mistake that we noted and corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And therefore, according to the document, you instructed Mr. Jesuric to carry out all preparations in connection with the takeover of the CSB and advise the government of Majevica and Semberija?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law on the interior of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a centre was formed, a district centre for Majevica and Semberija, for all the work that had to do with the interior, the MUP. Ugljevik was a mistake. So the headquarters, the seat, were transferred from Ugljevik to Bijeljina, because it's a bigger town. It has the proper equipment. So I officially informed this Mr. Jesuric about it, because even before the war, he was head of the MUP in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated earlier that when you became deputy minister of the MUP, you were headquartered in Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Vrace, but Mico Stanisic, as minister, was in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what were your duties and what role did you discharge during the time you were deputy minister in Vrace?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received all my instructions and assignments from Minister Mico Stanisic. I did whatever he ordered me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as a general matter, what did you do during that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an example of what I did on Mico Stanisic's instructions, that is to say, to inform Jesuric that the centre is in Bijeljina rather than Ugljevik and that this was a typographical error in the law on the interior and we informed both Jesuric and the government about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you direct war operations during that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you engaged with the national security and police services in connection with war operations in Grbavica, Dobrinja, Ilidza, the surroundings of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together with me at Vrace was the commander of the special unit, and the special unit itself, from the ranks of the Serb people. And it is possible that I took part in decision-making, or rather, in terms of the use of special units in the areas of Dobrinja, Vrace, Grbavica and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could the witness please be asked to speak a little slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you're asked to speak slower, because the interpreters have difficulties following your speed. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you indicated that it was possible -- let me direct your attention, then, back to Exhibit 419. And Mr. Mandic, I appreciate that the exhibit placed before you is in the English language, so I will have to read you the portion slowly so it can be translated for you. I'll be directing your attention and counsel's attention and the Court's attention to the passage contained on the bottom of page 10 of the English translation, beginning at the section marked 5230 of the video. And to refresh your recollection, Mr. Mandic, although you may be able to tell from the English version alone, this was an interview July and August of 1994, conducted by Mr. Djogo on the programme "My Guest is Truth." And you said at that portion: "I stayed for a month on Vrace, you know. People came. We formed services. I was working. Mico Stanisic coordinated between President Karadzic, who was on Pale at that moment, and I was on Vrace with the members of the special unit. We accepted --" a question mark behind that word "-- our national security, police services, liberated the neighbourhoods of Grbavica, Dobrinja, Ilidza, and communicating with Slobo Kovac [sic], who did Ilidza extremely well, as well as some other people from Serbian Sarajevo, Ilijas, Hadzici, Pale and other parts of Sarajevo." Mr. Mandic, does that refresh your recollection about your participation in efforts during the month of April or during the time you were on Vrace to "liberate the neighbourhoods of Grbavica, Dobrinja, Ilidza" through operations involving those forces?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this pertains to the Serb police in the area of Sarajevo. Ilidza, Hadzici, and Pale belonged to that municipality. This does not mean that it was some kind of cleansing. This was a takeover by the Serb police in those areas, and here in Ilidza, Tomislav Kovac was the chief of police in Ilidza. The name is wrong here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there war operations in those municipalities that resulted in the capture and detention of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I was at Vrace only for a month. Then I went to Pale, where I became minister of justice. I spent a very short period of time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did you mean when you talked about the liberation of the neighbourhoods of Grbavica, Dobrinja, and Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably together with these crisis staffs of these areas, the Serbs took over power in Ilijas, Hadzici, Grbavica. I assume that that's the way it was. This interview was -- took place 14 years ago, so I assume that that is what was meant by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you one of the strategists of war operations in connection with the liberation of Grbavica, Dobrinja, Ilidza, or any other aspects of the effort to establish Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you regarded by members of the Assembly as -- or any other persons in authority in Republika Srpska, as a war strategist?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, it was the army that mapped the war strategy in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So special MUP units were under the command of the army. So there is no way I could have been the chief strategist in Bosnia or in Sarajevo, because in the beginning of April, Ratko Mladic became chief of staff, and he took over all responsibility in terms of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the transcript indicates that you said that Ratko Mladic became Chief of Staff at the beginning of April. Is that in fact the date you recall, at the beginning of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The month of April 1992. That's for sure, that he became commander then, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in connection with the questions I asked about your -- the question I asked about you as war strategist, let me direct your attention to another exhibit, and that's a portion of the 16th Assembly session of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, held on the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Mandic, do you recall being present at the 16th session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina in Banja Luka on May 12th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention and the Court's attention to page 3 of the English translation, and I believe -- in any event, it's item 14 of the agenda. Was that the date on which your position as minister of justice was confirmed by the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of May, I was appointed minister of justice, I think. I was appointed when it was published in the Official Gazette. That's probably the date, but I do not recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me now direct your attention to the remarks of a member of the Assembly, Beli, contained on --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we be clear whether it's the Prosecution's position that Mr. Mandic was or wasn't at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, I think it's about to become abundantly clear. Second, the witness said he didn't recall. I think it's appropriate for me to attempt to refresh his recollection with a portion of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wasn't saying it wasn't, Your Honour. What Mr. Tieger is saying he's about to make clear is exactly what I was asking to be made clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, therefore, the position of the Prosecution is clear. It would have been clear, I take it. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Your Honour. It's not yet clear to me. That's what apparently was about to be made clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you're confronted with which part exactly of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I think that's an unnecessary intervention and it would have been completely clear. I had directed the Court's attention to page 16 of the English translation, the re-marks of Mr. Beli.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Mandic, that begins on page 10 of the B/C/S version you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour. I asked a very simple question which is whether it is the Prosecution's position that Mr. Mandic was or wasn't at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Stewart, from what I understand from Mr. Tieger, that he'll draw the attention to the text, especially on page 17, where it becomes abundantly clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that now. Thank you very much. And Ms. Cmeric has just drawn it to my attention. We could have got there a lot quicker if Mr. Tieger had just said yes. I can't see every word at every moment. I asked a simple question to which a simple answer would have been yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it would have been just as clear without the intervention. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Mandic, let me direct your attention to a particular part of Mr. Beli's remarks that appear approximately in the middle of his comments, where he says: "To keep it brief, I would like to ask that we do not leave this place without, and above all, the military strategist. I see Mr. Mandic is here. Without having some problem areas such as Brcko or Derventa precisely defined in military terms so that we know Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond where to turn for help."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Was this a different Mandic perhaps? Could you please tell me what page you were quoting from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's on page 10 of the version you have in front of you, Mr. Mandic. And if you -- the identities of the speakers are indicated at the beginning of their comments on the left in capital letters and it's -- Beli, yes. And the comments to which I'm referring appear in approximately the middle of his remarks.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is a different person here. There is a Mandic from Ugljevik who was some kind of military officer. It's certainly not me. Mr. Prosecutor, I think that you simply misidentified the person involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the Mandic to whom Mr. Beli is referring is who, according to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the man has the last name -- the same last name and from Ugljevik. He was some kind of local leader, or rather, he was a radical. So I think that's the mistake. Mistaken identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must -- with respect, I must persist with the inquiry that I'm making, because again this is the Prosecution's witness. The witness says he can't recall. Is it going to be the Prosecution's case that Mr. Mandic was at the meeting, wasn't at the meeting or that the Prosecution cannot say and is therefore entirely neutral at the moment as to whether he was or he wasn't? Because it does, after all, make quite a difference when a witness is going to be apparently questioned in relation to a particular meeting of which we have pages and pages of transcript, whether the questioning is proceeding on the footing that he was there or wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you now answer the question. Because now we have a situation which is a bit different from three minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I'd be happy to, Your Honour. Number one, I don't think it's incumbent on the Prosecution to take a particular position on the question of Mr. Mandic's presence unless additional questions are asked about events at that particular Assembly. It was clear I was asking that question in connection with Mr. Mandic's role while deputy minister and while headquartered in Vrace. And that was the nature of the question that was asked. We have an answer to that question now. I'm moving on to other areas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you are relatively -- I mean, you asked a question about his presence. I take it that you assumed that on the basis of that observation by one of those present during the meeting that Mr. Mandic would have been there as well, but at the same time, do I understand you that since Mr. Mandic says it was not a person that you now leave that open at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. I'm note going to make an issue of that at the moment, regardless of what other evidence may or may not disclose during the course of this case. Let me say also that -- maybe this is an useful opportunity, although, to draw a line. I haven't been objecting to objections. However, I think there comes a point at which constant interventions that are unnecessary become disruptive in a manner that impedes both the efficiency of the court and the court's opportunity to hear evidence. And I would appreciate counsel waiting for cross-examination if he has questions, or waiting until the conclusion of at least a portion of the questioning process during examination-in-chief before making interventions that effectively disrupt the flow of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the positions are the parties are clear to the extent that Mr. Stewart thinks that he should intervene whenever he thinks that necessary; at the same time, Mr. Stewart may have noticed that the Chamber would not always agree on the necessity of the intervention. Sometimes, Mr. Tieger, the Chamber followed some suggestions by Mr. Stewart. Both parties are invited not to disrupt the flow of evidence unless there's a real necessity. But I'm doing it at this moment myself, Mr. Tieger. I have some difficulties to reconcile the first page of these minutes in English and what I see in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to disrupt by mentioning exactly that point, Your Honour. We're missing I think three pages of B/C/S. There isn't a B/C/S translation of the first three pages of this particular -- four pages, I'm told -- of this document, which is in fact Your Honour anticipated me by about five seconds there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please take care that we have the same document in English and in B/C/S, and please find out what the difference exactly is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. And this may -- perhaps this shouldn't receive a separate exhibit number in any event, in view of the fact that I think this is -- this was introduced during the course of Mr. Treanor's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we might not have read every single page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, and I think therefore we'll be able to resolve the discrepancy the Court just noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Your Honour, so far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you'll check, then, during the next break the P65 and then tab 127.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I observe, Your Honour. Mr. Mandic, we believe, has only had from page 5 onwards or the equivalent B/C/S of what we see in the English from page 5 onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, it seems to start the same, to be the minutes of the 16th session and then who is presiding, and then suddenly it becomes different. Is that -- or do I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It seems that the first few pages are some sort of summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever it is, we would have to -- these first pages might not be in the -- might not be focused upon. But please take care, Mr. Tieger, that we have the same documents in English and in B/C/S. About whether they get a separate number or not, we'll first await your observations in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can I ask you next to take a look at the Prosecution's next in order, which is an article from February of 1998 that appeared in Oslobodjenje. That's ET 0093-8152.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the Defence would make any observation as far as the title of the -- the translation of the title is concerned, it would not surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes. Well, we make the obvious observation that Your Honour implies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We don't know where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, it's -- this article seems to start at the right top something about Momcilo Mandic, and then it has got something to do with the BiH MUP. Nothing of that kind appears in the translation. Then the main title seems to be "Wrong policy," and I have some doubt as to whether "Radovanova pogresna politica" is exactly just "wrong policy."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can certainly see the point the Court is making. That will have to be corrected and I apologise for that translation error. It appears to me from the rest of the article the translation corresponds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll ask the Defence and especially Ms. Cmeric to Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond keep a close eye on all those portions of the article which are put to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I wanted to direct your attention to a portion of the article that appears about two thirds down, after a discussion of -- and I'm going to mention a couple of names to help you identify that portion of the article more easily. There's a discussion about Ejup Ganic, and then Ratko Mladic and then Mr. Karadzic; and then Ms. Plavsic are mentioned in short succession. Do you see that portion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then the article goes on to say the following -- After you comment about Mrs. -- well, let me start it at that portion. Perhaps it will be easier: "I also mentioned the thing when Ejup Ganic took the state security from us using these technical devices that we lost on that occasion. They recorded Ratko Mladic and Karadzic, which is now the main evidence to The Hague. Well, we had to release 5.000 imprisoned Muslims for the family of Biljana Plavsic, and she was in Belgrade. She has got a flat in Vracar. She was the first one to get a flat whereas I, a minister, was wearing a flak jacket and taking part in combats in Dobrinja as a soldier. I was a minister up to 2.00 and I took part in actions in the afternoon." Mr. Mandic, does that refresh your recollection about your duties and role during the time you were at Vrace as deputy minister?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you keep supplying me with newspaper articles where I seem to inflate my role with respect to Biljana Plavsic. Because there was this conflict going on between her and myself since 1991, when she was a Presidency member. So I never did actually wear a flak jacket or fight, because at Dobrinja and when I was at Vrace, I wasn't able to go anywhere else. And then I moved to Pale and Hotel Bistrica Jakonina [phoen], as the minister of justice. So these are newspaper articles that you keep showing me, and as such, I don't think that you should give -- lend too much importance to the statements made here in these articles, if they are indeed my own statements. Because I was criticising Radovan Karadzic in actual fact, his -- the wrong policy he was pursuing, and his agreement to have the MUP enter into corruption, crimes, and that the perpetrators and so on. Radovan Karadzic and myself didn't see eye to eye on this point. And I went to Belgrade afterwards on the 2nd of December. That's the truth. Now, in each of these articles, the ones you've presented me with, you have relationships between myself and Mrs. Plavsic which were bad. We were in conflict. I said that I -- and then I exaggerated the extent to which I worked for the Serb cause, and said that Biljana sent her family to Belgrade and so on and that in hospitals where wounded people were put up, that she had accommodated her relations there. So this was all the result of that conflict that we had going on between us. And you've pulled this out of context, out of the interview, the entire interview, when I speak about the weaknesses of Radovan Karadzic's leadership, corruption, crime, and everything else that forced me to leave and go to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think you just indicated that you didn't wear a flak jacket. Did you monitor, coordinate, direct, or otherwise get involved with operations in Dobrinja, Grbavica, Ilidza, or the surrounding areas in Sarajevo during April and May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can turn to some of the recordings that you referred to in the article we just looked at. You referred to recordings using devices of people who were talking. Let's turn, then, to a couple of contemporaneous telephone intercepts. The first is 0322-0086.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]: Tomislav KOVAC: Hello. Momcilo MANDIC: Momo Mandic on the phone. Who's there? Tomislav KOVAC: Momo, Tomo here. Momcilo MANDIC: Tomo how are you? Tomislav KOVAC: Well. Momcilo MANDIC: Tell me, what's up in Ilidza? Tomislav KOVAC: Fuck, a lot. Momcilo MANDIC: Are there big problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's no B/C/S, I think, Your Honour, coming across.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not hear anything, and therefore, so no translation. I think we best restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Since we're going to do that, perhaps I can introduce this exhibit a little bit more fully. It's a conversation that takes place on the 23rd of April, 1992, between Mr. Mandic and Mr. Tomo Kovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And on the bottom of the page it says it's the first out of 6 and all together I think there are three pages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The audio will be P429 and the transcript will be P429A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's restart. [Intercept played]. Momcilo MANDIC: What was the telephone number in Ilidza again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]: Tomislav KOVAC: Hello. Momcilo MANDIC: Momo Mandic on the phone. Who's there? Tomislav KOVAC: Momo, Tomo here. Momcilo MANDIC: Tomo, how are you? Tomislav KOVAC: Well. Momcilo MANDIC: Tell me, what's up in Ilidza? Tomislav KOVAC: Fuck, a lot. Momcilo MANDIC: Are there big problems?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stops at the same moment. We're close to a quarter to 2.00, Mr. Tieger. Would you have any further questions unrelated to this to the witness? If not, perhaps we would otherwise adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the next exhibit is also an intercept, Your Honour, and whether or not we have the same problem, I don't know, but I don't think we'd get through it in five minutes, in fairness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'd better adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I observe. Apparently, and I think it's fairly plain, in fact, the introductory lines under the heading "English translation" contain one or two remarks which are not strictly translation. The bits in brackets "(RS Minister of Justice)" and brackets after Tomo, "(Ilidza para-police commander)", those are not taken from the B/C/S. They've been added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand this, Mr. Stewart, and although you know that I'm very fond of precise translations, if we have it on the record, would it be sufficient? Because otherwise it has to be reprinted again, which takes not only ink but also paper and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're keen on precision, but also I ought to make it clear I'm not asking for it to be redone; I am as Your Honour is indicating, just putting it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's on the record now. Is there any further procedural issue to be raised at this moment? If not, we'll adjourn for the day. Mr. Mandic, I'd like to give you the same instructions as I did yesterday, that is, not to speak with anyone, not to communicate with anyone, so that's not only speech but also e-mails and the like, about the testimony you have given and you're still about to give. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom. Yes. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of November, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
